title: A Helping Hand

contributors.contribution: Handled sales and helped bring the product to funeral-home customers.
Invested in the company and participated as partners in the business.

description: A Helping Hand was a commercial Windows estate-planning application that I co-developed with a friend during the early years of CD Software Developers. The application was built primarily in Visual Basic 6 and used OLE/ActiveX-era Windows technologies, database-backed content, rich-text interfaces, navigation trees, forms, printing, and supporting automation components. A surviving source snapshot dates to 2002, while a Version 1.0 CD distribution is documented from March 2004.

sections.title: Commercial Desktop Application
paragraphs: A Helping Hand was developed as a packaged Windows application intended for distribution to funeral homes and their customers.
The software organized estate-planning information, reference material, financial topics, forms, and related guidance inside a structured desktop interface.

sections.title: Visual Basic 6 Application
paragraphs: The surviving source is a Visual Basic 6 project rather than VB.NET.
The application used traditional VB6 forms, modules, classes, ActiveX controls, OLE automation, and Windows APIs.

sections.title: Database & Data Access
paragraphs: The application used Microsoft's ADO-era data-access stack, including ADO and ADOX components, along with Jet-related database technology.

sections.title: Desktop UI
paragraphs: The application used a multi-pane Windows interface with hierarchical navigation, rich formatted content, menus, dialogs, forms, and supporting reference tools.

sections.title: OLE / Automation Components
paragraphs: The project used OLE and ActiveX-era integration patterns typical of Windows desktop software of the period.
The surviving source also includes a separate VB6 project that built an OLE DLL supporting the application.

sections.title: Distribution & Installation
paragraphs: The application was distributed on CD with a Windows installer and supporting installation documentation.
The confirmed Version 1.0 distribution is dated March 28, 2004 and supported Windows 95, 98, Me, 2000, and XP.

sections.title: Early Business Experience
paragraphs: The project was also part of my early experience as a software-business stakeholder.
I became a shareholder in CD Software Developers while helping build a real commercial product intended for sale to funeral homes.

sections.title: Project Timeline
paragraphs: The surviving source snapshot appears to represent the application around 2002.

Later documentation confirms a Version 1.0 CD build in March 2004. I do not treat that as evidence of two full years of continuous development; the later period may have included smaller edits, content changes, testing, packaging, and installer work.

historicalNotes: A Helping Hand was developed during the early years of CD Software Developers and sold/distributed for use by funeral homes.
Jamie co-developed the application with a friend and became a shareholder in the company.
The surviving source snapshot is Visual Basic 6 source, not VB.NET.
The main surviving VB6 project builds HelpingHand.exe.
The source uses VB6 forms/modules/classes and OLE/ActiveX-era Windows technologies.
The surviving code references ADO, ADOX, Jet-related components, RichTextBox, FlexGrid, CommonDialog, media controls, and Windows API calls.
A second VB6 project builds an OLE DLL used as part of the application architecture.
Source/project metadata strongly anchors the surviving code to 2002.
A Version 1.0 README is dated March 28, 2004 and documents CD-ROM installation and Windows 95 through XP compatibility.
The README copyright is 2002-2004 CDSoftware Developers Inc.
Do not publicly imply that the application required two years of continuous development.
Safest chronology: application substantially built around 2002, potentially edited/maintained afterward, with a confirmed 2004 Version 1.0 CD distribution.
The 2004 build may represent packaging/installer/documentation work in addition to or instead of major application-code changes.
CD Software Developers had seven partners associated with this project/business: Jamie, one additional developer, two sales partners, and three investor partners.
All seven participants were partners in the business.
Jamie was one of the two developers and also a shareholder/partner.
